name: Laopang
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Edmondson & Ziwo 1999, 'Laghuu' phonological study (Glottolog treats Laopang as duplicate of Laghuu [lgh]); not reachable online

sources.note: laop1234: 'This entry has been retired... There appears to be only one language in the literature that can match these characteristics, namely Xa-Pho of Abadie 1924:185-186 who testifies they call themselves Lao-pa. However, this language already has an entry... as Laghuu [lgh] (cf. Edmondson & Ziwo 1999)'. No descriptive references attached to laop1234.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 registration authority, code record lbg 'Laopang'.
sources.note: Code still Active (individual, living); no retirement/change request shown. Identity record only.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Laopan language' and 'Laghuu language' (wikitext via API).
sources.note: Laopan page: Bisoid, Bun Tay District, Phongsaly, autonym law33 pan11 ba11, cites Kingsadā & Shintani 1999 and Wright n.d. (ms.); Laghuu page summarises Edmondson & Lama 1999 (5 tones, disyllabic compounds) and supplied the sealang URL. Neither says anything about stress.

sources.citation: Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds.). 2016. Ethnologue 19th ed., entry 'Laopang' [lbg] (Wayback capture).
sources.note: 'A language of Laos... Alternate Names Laopa. Population 9,550 (2000). Location Bokeo province.... Classification Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Ngwi-Burmese, Ngwi, Unclassified. Typology SOV.' No sources, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2003. Three Tibeto-Burman languages of Vietnam. In D. Bradley et al. (eds.), Language variation: Papers on variation and change in the Sinosphere and in the Indosphere in honour of James A. Matisoff (PL 555), 305-320. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. Sect. 4 'Xa Pho, Laghuu, or Phu La Lao' pp. 311-314.
sources.note: Xa Pho initials, rhymes, nasal codas; 'Xa Pho has only one rising tone with the value 24. The other tones have the shapes 54, 44, 33, and 21' (p. 313). No stress statement. SILENT.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2002. The Central and Southern Loloish languages of Vietnam. Proceedings of BLS 28, Special Session on Tibeto-Burman and Southeast Asian Linguistics, 1-13.
sources.note: Xa Pho only named in the introduction as covered elsewhere; the paper treats Coong, Sila, Lahu, Hani. Nothing on Laghuu/Laopang stress.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. & Lama Ziwo. 1999. Laghuu or Xá Phó, a new language of the Yi group. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 22(1): 1-10.
sources.note: Sect. 2.0-2.5 (pp. 3-6): initials, rhymes, nasal codas, glides, five tones (55, 44, 33, 21, 24), sandhi 21>24 before 33, 55 becomes 54/53 word-finally; 'words are typically disyllabic compounds'. Nothing on stress or accent. SILENT.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1996. Tibeto-Burman languages of PDR Lao. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 19(1): 19-27.
sources.note: Table 1 (p. 19) lists 'Lao Pane' as one of the officially enumerated subgroups of the Phu Noy (Phunoi) ethnic group of Laos; Phunoi is Bisoid. Ethnic/classificatory survey only; no phonology, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Abadie, Maurice. 1924. Les races du Haut-Tonkin de Phong-Tho à Lang-Son. Paris: Société d'Éditions Géographiques, Maritimes et Coloniales. 'Les Xa-pho', pp. 185-186.
sources.note: 'Ces tribus se nomment elles-mêmes des Lao-pa'... 'Le dialecte a beaucoup d'analogies avec le dialecte fou-la'. Ethnographic; no linguistic description, nothing on accent. This is the sole basis for Glottolog's Laopang = Laghuu identification.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 2007. East and Southeast Asia. In Christopher Moseley (ed.), Encyclopedia of the World's Endangered Languages, 349-424. London: Routledge.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held

sources.note: Bradley's inventory of Laos Loloish groups is the likely origin of Ethnologue's 'Laopang, 9,550 (2000)' figure and would state which language he means by Laopang.

sources.citation: Kingsadā, Thō̜ngphet & Tadahiko Shintani (eds.). 1999. Basic vocabularies of the languages spoken in Phongxaly, Lao P.D.R. Lao-Japan Project Data paper 1. Tokyo: ILCAA.

sources.note: The source Ethnologue/Wikipedia rely on for the Laos 'Laopan' (Bun Tay, Phongsaly) identity; a transcribed wordlist would show whether the Laos Laopan is a Phunoi (Bisoid) variety, and any introductory phonological note might mark tone/stress. Only route to the Laos-side identity.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1977. Phunoi or Côông. In D. Bradley (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics No. 5 (PL A-49), 67-98. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.

sources.citation: Nguyễn Văn Huy. 1975. Bước đầu tìm hiểu mối quan hệ tộc người giữa hai nhóm Phù Lá và 'Xá Phó'. In Về vấn đề xác định thành phần các dân tộc thiểu số ở miền bắc Việt Nam, 415-428. Hà Nội: NXB Khoa học Xã hội.
